title: French Drama Series ‘The Red and the Black’: Passion, Power, Political Intrigue and Victor Belmondo’s Anti-Romantic Hero
summary: “The Red and the Black,” an adaptation of Stendhal’s 1830 novel, follows the young Julien Sorel (Victor Belmondo) as he pursues greatness, rising socially beyond his modest upbringing while entangled in a web of passion, power and political intrigue. Following screenings at Canneseries and the Italian Global Series Festival, “The Red and the Black,” produced […]
content:
“The Red and the Black,” an adaptation of Stendhal’s 1830 novel, follows the young Julien Sorel (Victor Belmondo) as he pursues greatness, rising socially beyond his modest upbringing while entangled in a web of passion, power and political intrigue.

Following screenings at Canneseries and the Italian Global Series Festival, “The Red and the Black,” produced by Siècle Productions for France Télévisions, makes its international market debut at the Unifrance Rendez-Vous in Le Havre, where it’s being sold by Wild Bunch.

The four-part series is directed by Gaël Morel, who reunites with Belmondo following their acclaimed 2024 relationship drama “To Live, to Die, to Live Again,” and written by Georges-Marc Benamou and Gilles Taurand, whose previous collaborations include “The Last Mitterrand” and more recently “The Plague.”

Popular on Variety

Credit: Nicolas Velter/France Télévisions/Siècle Productions/Wild Bunch

The creators found inspiration in the enduring qualities of Stendhal’s work.

“There is a universality to great literature, particularly 19th century French and Anglo-Saxon literature, from Stendhal to Jane Austen, who was almost Stendhal’s contemporary,” Benamou tells Variety.

“We can see young audiences going to cinemas to watch these adaptations again. It is literature of intense passions: free in its tone, its depiction of love, and its drama, yet often avoiding romantic sentimentality. In Stendhal’s case, Julien Sorel, the protagonist, is precisely an anti-romantic hero: an ambitious man whose aspirations are thwarted. That is what makes him both compelling and tragic.”

The story of an ambitious and calculating young man of modest origins trying to establish himself in circles of power dominated by ruthless and manipulative actors and confronted by great moral hypocrisy could very well be a tale of the 21st century.

The renowned work’s timeless themes have led to several big and small-screen adaptations over the decades, including Claude Autant-Lara’s 1954 version starring Gérard Philipe and the 1993 BBC series featuring Ewan McGregor in one of his earliest roles.

“There are indeed parallels with the present day,” Benamou adds. “This is part of the genius, and, once again, the universal appeal, of a great writer such as Stendhal, who was a dissenting voice in his own time.

“The parallels are clear: the return of moral conservatism, embodied by the Congregation of Catholic fundamentalists determined to destroy Julien Sorel; women constrained by society who choose to emancipate themselves; and the social determinism faced by this class defector, who is unable to escape his background. All of this, the resurgence of moral conservatism, stalled social mobility, and women’s emancipation, still resonates today in France, Europe and America.”

Morel stresses that the series “speaks more directly to contemporary issues: class defection, social determinism, and male–female relationships, which are especially modern in this work.

“Julien Sorel rises through society thanks to women, because they embody power. I think that the theme of class defection is at the heart of the modernity. Someone like Julien Sorel, struggling to rise through society, raises questions that remain very relevant in France today, particularly when we speak of social mobility, which may be even more stuck now than it was then.

“Unfortunately, it is a theme that remains contemporary and is likely to do so for a long time. Several of its themes therefore resonate with current events. There is also the return of obscurantism, embodied by the ‘black’ in the title.”

While enthusiastically embracing the material and its enduring themes, the production team faced a major task in transposing such a rich and complex novel into a television series.

“The abundance of characters, settings, social classes and novelistic digressions made this a challenging work to adapt,” Morel explains.

“So, I would describe it as a variation on the novel rather than a faithful adaptation. Our aim was to focus on several aspects of the story and draw from them a clear, coherent storyline.

“The themes we chose to foreground strike me as remarkably contemporary. Gilles Taurand and Georges-Marc Benamou’s clever work, applying the conventions of serial storytelling to this variation, has given the work a much-needed ‘rejuvenation’ while remaining deeply faithful to its spirit.”

In casting “The Red and the Black,” the production team found their ideal lead in Belmondo, particularly for their more authentic take on the character of Julien Sorel. The cast also includes Camille Razat (“Emily in Paris”) and Virginie Ledoyen (“At Work”).

“Victor Belmondo’s great strength lies in the fact that he is an outstanding young actor who has developed a relationship of friendship and trust with director Gaël Morel,” Benamou notes. “This is their second film together, and Gaël and I felt that, with Victor, we wanted to find an ‘anti-Gérard Philipe.’ The distinctly romantic image associated with Claude Autant-Lara’s 1954 film has, to some extent, overshadowed Stendhal’s work. We wanted to return to the origins of Julien Sorel: a man whose ambition is thwarted both by his own limitations and by those imposed by others, an anti-romantic hero.”

Morel adds: “Victor Belmondo immediately struck me as the ideal Julien Sorel. His youthfulness and intensity, together with his ability to convey a brooding, determined quality, provide the perfect vehicle for capturing the essence of the character.

“Sorel is not a romantic hero, although he may adopt that persona to seduce. Behind his youth and impoverished social background lies a fierce ambition and an almost pathological need for recognition. This interpretation of the character, as a calculating, seductive, boastful young man who sees life as a conquest, seems to me the most accurate. It is far removed from the romantic, victim-like figure that has sometimes been presented in earlier adaptations.”

For Wild Bunch, “The Red and the Black” epitomizes what it sees as ideal content.

“While brand recognition is important, our ambition goes further: to develop a deep understanding of the constantly evolving needs of our international buyers and propose programs that deliver strong audience appeal while bringing families together around a shared story,” says Diana Bartha, head of international sales and acquisitions at Wild Bunch.

“‘The Red and the Black’ ticks all the boxes. Universal and modern, it appeals to audiences across generations and offers the familiarity of a well-established concept alongside a fresh, contemporary take. Its broad appeal, strong emotional connection and ability to unite viewers make it the ideal series for this season — one that needs no introduction.”

title: Gaza Cinema Academy Launches at Venice Film Festival
summary: A group of prominent Palestinian, Arab and international filmmakers and industry professionals on Monday launched the Gaza Cinema Academy at the Venice Film Festival. The new entity aims to establish a sustainable space for film education, training and production in Gaza, “while connecting emerging Palestinian filmmakers with the wider international film community,” as a statement […]
content:
A group of prominent Palestinian, Arab and international filmmakers and industry professionals on Monday launched the Gaza Cinema Academy at the Venice Film Festival. The new entity aims to establish a sustainable space for film education, training and production in Gaza, “while connecting emerging Palestinian filmmakers with the wider international film community,” as a statement put it.

The Gaza Cinema Academy is being supported by 2025 Venice Silver Lion winner — and Venice jury member — Kaouther Ben Hania (“The Voice of Hind Rajab”) and fellow directors Annemarie Jacir (“Palestine 36″), Mai Masri (“3000 Nights”) — who is the academy’s co-founder — and Ezzaldeen Shalah, as well as actors Hiam Abbas, Ramy Youssef and Saleh Bakri. Italian producer Graziella Bildesheim and Cairo-based distributor and Arab film industry promoter Alaa Karkouti are also on board.

The academy will focus “on film education and training, supporting young talent and women, developing and producing new Palestinian films, strengthening the presence of filmmakers in Gaza and their connections with the Palestinian, Arab and international film communities, and building a sustainable film institution in the Gaza Strip,” the statement said.

Popular on Variety

They are seeking to build a rapport with film festivals and other cultural institutions, as well as film funds, and production companies. “The academy aspires to build an international network of partners that supports emerging film talent in Gaza, strengthens opportunities for learning and production, and helps their films reach festivals, platforms and audiences around the world,” it noted.

“In Gaza, cinema is not merely an art form; it is a means of preserving memory, reclaiming our right to shape our own image, and giving a new generation the tools to tell its own story,” said Shalah, who is founder of the Gaza International Women’s Film Festival and co-founder of the Gaza Cinema Academy, in the statement. “We want the academy to open a window for young people and women in Gaza to learn, create and make their own films, and for their voices and images to reach the world. We invite our partners in institutions, universities and the international film community to be part of building this space.“

The first edition of the Gaza International Women’s Film Festival was held Oct. 26-31, 2025, amid rubble in the heart of the Gaza strip. The Gaza fest opened with “The Voice of Hind Rajab.”

There are two Palestinian films in Venice’s official selection this year: Ahmed Hassouna’s “Citizen Osama,” which portrays a photographer (film still above) as he attempts to juggle his roles as father and a journalist while capturing the realities of war in Gaza; and Muayad Alayan’s “Conversation With the Sea,” about a 60-year-old Palestinian man named Kamal who becomes entangled in a tendentious web of Israeli bureaucracy.

title: Tsai Ming-liang on Venice and San Sebastian Title ‘Dust,’ Slowness as Rebellion and Life With Lee Kang-sheng
summary: A barefoot monk in a red robe walks the length of San Sebastian’s La Concha, pauses beneath the concrete rooms of Chillida Leku and stands before the crashing wall of the Peine del Viento. He is Tsai Ming-liang’s Walker, and in “Dust,” the 11th installment of the director’s “Walker” series, his slow procession moves through […]
content:
A barefoot monk in a red robe walks the length of San Sebastian’s La Concha, pauses beneath the concrete rooms of Chillida Leku and stands before the crashing wall of the Peine del Viento. He is Tsai Ming-liang‘s Walker, and in “Dust,” the 11th installment of the director’s “Walker” series, his slow procession moves through Spain for the first time.

The film debuts at the Venice Film Festival, then moves to the San Sebastian Film Festival.

Produced by Vitrine Filmes and Homegreen Films, with backing from the Basque regional government’s culture and language department, the Taiwan Public Television Service Foundation and Tabakalera, “Dust” continues a project Tsai launched in 2012 built around a single recurring image: Lee Kang-sheng walking in near-stillness through unfamiliar cities, his body tracing how a place is felt and moved through over time.

Popular on Variety

Tsai traces the whole project back to a stage production more than a decade ago, where a slow-walking performance by Lee left a lasting mark on him. “At the time, I had grown tired of making narrative films, and Lee’s slow walk gave me the idea of making something non-narrative, a form of pure visual expression,” he says. “The way he walks is extraordinarily beautiful, and the idea of ‘slowness’ itself has great power.” What still strikes him, after 15 years of filming the same gesture, is Lee’s physical control: “He is still able to maintain the same power he had at the very beginning.”

Spain entered the picture through a co-production partner. Tsai says he scouted San Sebastian twice before settling on it, taken with the city itself but even more with what surrounded it: “Basque stone houses, an abandoned mining tunnel, the tremendous force of the waves crashing against the Peine del Viento, the sound of church bells surrounding San Sebastian and the face of an elderly Basque farmer.”

That patience is, for Tsai, the whole point of the exercise. Cinema, he argues, has trained audiences to treat images as information to be processed rather than looked at. “Slowness may simply be a method: it allows you to become quiet, to really look and to feel — to gaze at a face, an object, an event,” he says. “Slowness, in fact, is also a form of rebellion.”

The series has by now carried the Walker from Taipei and Hong Kong through two further shorts shot at a Yunlin exhibition space, on to Kuching, Malaysia; Marseille, France; Tokyo; the Taiwan‘s Yilan coast; Paris; and Washington, D.C., before this latest journey to San Sebastian, and Tsai describes him as a kind of instrument for reading a place. Every city, he says, carries its own atmosphere and pace, and Lee’s shaved head, bare feet and red robe throw that character into relief. In San Sebastian, what caught him was the light: “The sunlight constantly shifting between brightness and shadow, falling across enormous sculptures, forests, streets, pedestrians and the Walker’s red robe. It is very beautiful.”

Underneath the travelogue is a much longer collaboration. Tsai and Lee have worked together for more than 30 years, and the director speaks of the series as something closer to a document of aging than a formal experiment. “We have watched Lee Kang-Sheng’s body, appearance, and even his skin change,” he says. “Only through looking at someone over a long period of time can the reality of a life be fully revealed. To have been able to keep filming Lee Kang-Sheng is the greatest gift heaven has given me.”

Venice has bookended Tsai’s career in its own way. “Vive L’Amour” won the Golden Lion there in 1994; “Dust” returns him to the festival with a film that shares almost nothing with it formally. Tsai frames the distance between the two less as a rupture than as an ongoing argument with the medium itself. Some assume he stopped making films, he says, simply because he stopped making the kind audiences expected: “In fact, I have never stopped making films. I have been searching for the possibilities of cinema: what else can cinema express, besides telling stories?” He questions whether the theater itself has grown too conservative a container: “It should be able to contain all kinds of films, not only narrative films or documentaries. The ‘Walker’ series is clearly neither fiction nor documentary. It is simply a form of cinema, and it deserves to be seen in a cinema.”

He’s less pessimistic about audiences than that argument might suggest. Tsai splits viewers into two camps — one seeking pure entertainment, another open to work that asks more of them — and says the second group hasn’t shrunk. “My films are screened in cities all over the world, and I have found that more and more young people are coming to see them.”

Working with a largely new Spanish crew, he says, didn’t require him to change anything. Tsai has long mixed his longtime Taiwanese team with international crews and film students, and this production was no exception: “I was very satisfied with the Spanish team this time, especially the two cinematographers. I really liked the way they handled the images.”

The series isn’t finished with him yet. The next “Walker” film will take him to Jeonju, Korea, on an invitation from the Jeonju Intl. Film Festival, and Tsai is untroubled by questions about where the project ends. “I think it will end only when either Lee Kang-Sheng or I am no longer here,” he says.

Beyond “Walker,” his ambitions have narrowed rather than faded. “I am getting older now, and I do not have the same energy I once had,” he says. “The one thing I still very much hope to do is to work once more with all the actors I have collaborated with over the years. Perhaps I will make one more narrative film that is not really a narrative film.”

Three decades after his Golden Lion, Tsai returns to Venice with a film that has no plot, no dialogue and, by his own account, no interest in changing that.

title: Sri Sri Ravi Shankar’s WFAC, Creativeland Take ‘Krishnavataram’ Global (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Sri Sri Ravi Shankar’s World Forum For Art and Culture (WFAC) and Creativeland Studios have formalized a partnership to take “Krishnavataram,” a trilogy tracing the life of Hindu God Lord Krishna, to international audiences. The association was made official on Janmashtami, the Hindu festival marking the birth of Lord Krishna and one of the most […]
content:
Sri Sri Ravi Shankar‘s World Forum For Art and Culture (WFAC) and Creativeland Studios have formalized a partnership to take “Krishnavataram,” a trilogy tracing the life of Hindu God Lord Krishna, to international audiences.

The association was made official on Janmashtami, the Hindu festival marking the birth of Lord Krishna and one of the most widely observed celebrations on the Hindu calendar. WFAC and Creativeland Studios finalized the deal in the presence of Ravi Shankar.

“Krishnavataram” is envisioned as a three-part retelling of Krishna’s life, with its chapters subtitled “Hridayam” (“The Heart”), “Manaha” (“The Mind”) and “Atman” (“The Soul”). The first installment, “Krishnavataram: Part 1 – Hridayam,” is directed by Hardik Gajjar and stars Siddharth Gupta as Krishna, with Sanskruti Jayana as Satyabhama, Sushmita Bhatt as Radha and Nivaashiyni Krishnan as Rukmini. The film has already had a run in Indian theaters, and the new partnership is aimed at carrying it to viewers abroad.

Popular on Variety

The rollout will begin with a wider theatrical release, reaching the Indian diaspora and international audiences in the Hindi, Tamil, Telugu and English languages. WFAC and Creativeland Studios also plan to extend “Krishnavataram” into series, music, live experiences, games, education and immersive cultural programming.

“Krishna means the most attractive the self. It is the divinity that is the most attractive; the energy that pulls everything to it. When you realize your life and the whole world is just a leela (play), then Krishna is born inside you,” Ravi Shankar said.

Producer Sajan Raj Kurup of Creativeland Studios described the partnership as an extension of Ravi Shankar’s influence on the project. “With the blessings of Gurudev Sri Sri Ravi Shankar, who has nurtured the entire world with his grace and transformed the lives of millions, this film finds its best place at the feet of Gurudev. With ‘Krishnavataram,’ we take pride in taking every bit of Indian culture to the world and presenting our cultural beliefs, which are a fundamental part of our very existence. Our vision is to build ‘Krishnavataram’ into a global cultural movement that celebrates cinema, art, and legacy,” Kurup said.

The partners describe the effort as an attempt to build a contemporary entry point into the Krishna story while staying grounded in the philosophical, artistic and cultural traditions the trilogy draws from. The international release of “Krishnavataram: Part 1 – Hridayam” is being positioned as the opening step in that broader push, with expansion into new formats framed as an ongoing effort rather than a single release.

title: AI Filmmaking’s Future Debated by Alibaba, Sonilo, PROMPTR Executives at TapNow and Dogme23’s Venice Production Bridge Panel
summary: Executives from Alibaba Token Hub, Sonilo and PROMPTR joined film educator Barry Dignam at a TapNow-hosted panel during the Venice Film Festival’s Venice Production Bridge to debate AI filmmaking’s creative and economic impact, capped by a technical breakdown of the AI-generated series “Primodia.” The panel, titled “AI x Cinema: The 10,000 Parallel Universes Initiative,” was […]
content:
Executives from Alibaba Token Hub, Sonilo and PROMPTR joined film educator Barry Dignam at a TapNow-hosted panel during the Venice Film Festival‘s Venice Production Bridge to debate AI filmmaking’s creative and economic impact, capped by a technical breakdown of the AI-generated series “Primodia.”

The panel, titled “AI x Cinema: The 10,000 Parallel Universes Initiative,” was held at Hotel Excelsior and cohosted with event organizer Dogme23. It was moderated by Sabrina Qin, brand lead at TapNow, the AI creative platform developed by California-based Tamar AI, which also operates the AI-native streaming platform Glanze TV. Panelists included Tianshu Zhu, head of global AI product solutions at Alibaba Token Hub; Dignam, vice dean of FilmEU at IADT and chair of the CILECT European chapter; Ben Chimoy, GenAI director at PROMPTR and founder of AI Filmmakers Berlin; and Shawn Song, co-founder and CEO of Sonilo, who previously led audio research at TikTok.

Chimoy, who spent 15 years in traditional filmmaking before moving into AI video, said his shift began while producing fashion films for Zalando. He said a client preferred an AI-generated version of a project over the final produced film because it felt more emotional, a reaction he called unexpected given AI’s reputation for being unemotional.

Popular on Variety

“For me, AI is actually connecting people, bringing us into the same room to create together,” Chimoy said.

Dignam, representing FilmEU’s network of 50 European film schools, argued that AI raises the stakes for film education rather than lowering them. He said schools should not try to teach every new tool, since the technology changes faster than curricula can be rebuilt.

“I do think we need to teach critical thinking and core values around craft and practice,” Dignam said.

“AI is not a shortcut to becoming a filmmaker. You still have to do the work,” he added.

Zhu said HappyHorse, the AI video generation model built by Alibaba Token Hub, is designed to address budget and resource constraints rather than an absence of good stories, with a focus on pre-production tasks such as storyboarding, 3D character placement and previsualization.

“I really resonated with you that filmmaking is never lacking a good story; it’s the budget, the resources, and obstacles, the languages that’s turning into real challenges,” Zhu said.

He said Alibaba Token Hub plans to launch HappyHorse 2.0 and a companion tool called HappyHorse Control, described as a “world model” enabling real-time interaction, by the end of September.

Song discussed Sonilo’s licensing agreements with Universal Music Group and Sony Music, which he said give commercial users confidence to use the company’s AI-generated music without publishing disputes, with revenue shared among the publisher, label company and creator.

“Not every song is a masterpiece. But every song represents someone’s time, effort, and dedication,” Song said.

TapNow used the panel to introduce its Creator Growth Plan, offering three tiers of entry. An Experimental Creator tier lets participants publish qualifying work on Tap TV, with exposure in more than 100 countries and access to unlimited open compute. A Selected Creator tier requires submitting a portfolio or social media channel for review. A Signed Creator tier is invitation-only, requiring a referral from an existing signed creator, and includes a guaranteed monthly minimum along with free compute and priority technical support.

The panel closed with a technical presentation on “Primodia,” an S-level flagship series in TapNow’s “10,000 Parallel Universes” initiative directed by Haonan Liu and Yuhang Qiao, described as first-time AI directors who had studied AI filmmaking for less than a year. Presenters said TapNow’s tools were used for early concept art and that its Creative OS agent generated video content directly through conversational prompts. A Sonilo representative said its tools helped cut composing time on the project.

“We reduced the composing time from 10 hours to 20 seconds,” the representative said.

Qin closed the session by framing the panel’s broader stakes for the industry.

“AI will not define the taste of future content, but creators will,” she said.

title: Emmys Night 2 Craft Awards Predict Smooth Sailing For ‘Widow’s Bay’ Alongside Celebrating ‘The Pitt’ & ‘DTF St. Louis’
summary: On Emmys Night 2, the Television Academy proved that it was, in fact, DTF St. Louis. During Sunday night’s ceremony, formally known as the Creative Arts Emmys, HBO’s limited drama series picked up four wins across craft categories with Outstanding Cinematography for a Limited or Anthology Series or Movie, Outstanding Picture Editing for a Limited […]
content:
On Emmys Night 2, the Television Academy proved that it was, in fact, DTF St. Louis.

During Sunday night’s ceremony, formally known as the Creative Arts Emmys, HBO’s limited drama series picked up four wins across craft categories with Outstanding Cinematography for a Limited or Anthology Series or Movie, Outstanding Picture Editing for a Limited or Anthology Series or Movie, Outstanding Directing for a Limited or Anthology Series or Movie and Outstanding Writing for a Limited or Anthology Series or Movie. David Harbour and Linda Cardellini then added to the haul with their first Emmy wins, taking Outstanding Supporting Actor and Outstanding Supporting Actress in a Limited or Anthology Series or Movie, respectively.

The two nights, which honor the bulk of its craft awards that recognize cinematographers, editors, casting directors, production designers, sound teams, makeup artists, costume design, stunt coordinators—and now supporting and guest actors—will be combined into a broadcast airing on Hulu and FXX on September 12 ahead of the live NBC and Peacock Primetime Emmys broadcast on September 14.

Watch on Deadline

And while the craft races don’t always provide a clear crystal ball for the televised Emmys, Sunday night did produce some surprising results that could potentially shake the table for once “safe” predictions.

Widow’s Bay had the strongest showing with eight wins. Unsurprising, considering that the Apple TV dark comedy horror series came into the fray with 19 nominations. But the word-of-mouth trojan horse held its own against the final season of Hacks and the cult-hit A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms as it picked up seven wins in the craft categories: Outstanding Casting for a Comedy Series, Outstanding Cinematography for a Series (Half-Hour), Outstanding Production Design for a Narrative Program (Half-Hour), Outstanding Sound Editing for a Comedy or Drama Series (Half-Hour) and Animation, Outstanding Sound Mixing for a Comedy or Drama Series (Half-Hour) and Animation, Outstanding Music Supervision, Outstanding Music Composition and Outstanding Music Composition for a Series (Original Dramatic Score). Betty Gilpin also won Outstanding Guest Actress in a Comedy Series.

Will being recognized across a variety of crafts instead of just one concentrated area carry over to a win for Outstanding Comedy Series toppling favorites like Abbott Elementary or Hacks, again, a show campaigning for its last season. Who’s to say? But these wins give the show a considerable awards-season story to take into the final stretch.

The heavily decorated medical drama The Pitt, nominated for a whopping 25 categories, picked up two below-the-line awards for Outstanding Prosthetic Makeup and Outstanding Casting for Drama Series. But even with its quiet night, Ernest Harden Jr. bested fellow fan-favorite nominees Colman Domingo and Jeff Hiller for his heartbreaking performance in The Pitt as Louie. Last year, The Pitt was nominated for 13 Emmys and took home five. We could see repeat wins for Noah Wyle and Outstanding Drama Series, nevertheless.

Then there was Spider-Noir, which had a bittersweet reason to celebrate. Just two days before the ceremony, Prime Video announced the series’ cancellation. The series spun a web to five Emmy wins, all in craft categories: Outstanding Cinematography for a Series (One Hour), Outstanding Special Visual Effects in a Single Episode, Outstanding Title Design, Outstanding Stunt Coordination for Comedy Programming and Outstanding Sound Editing for a Comedy or Drama Series (One Hour). Star Nicolas Cage, before the ceremony, has since responded to the cancellation, telling Deadline, “For me, one season is perfect, having said what I wanted to say with this dangerous, innovative, pop-art Spider-Man. Onwards, upwards, inwards.”

But it’s a wonder if Prime Video truly knows the meaning of “with great power comes great responsibility,” as a now-canceled series that collected five Emmys shows that voters were paying attention nonetheless. There is a small silver lining, however: perhaps Wonder Man star Yahya Abdul-Mateen II has a chance at winning despite Disney+’s cancellation of the series. The major difference here, though, is that Disney announced the series’ cancellation mere days before voting took place.

Elsewhere, Pluribus picked up four awards: Outstanding Period Costumes, Outstanding Production Design for a Narrative Period or Fantasy Program (One Hour or More), Outstanding Sound Editing for a Comedy or Drama Series (One Hour) and Outstanding Special Visual Effects in a Season or a Movie; Fallout won two, Outstanding Fantasy/Sci-Fi Costumes and Outstanding Special Visual Effects in a Season or a Movie, and A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms took Outstanding Stunt Performance.

For now, we will have to wait and see what the future holds.

The 78th Primetime Emmys will be held at the Peacock Theater in Downtown Los Angeles and will be hosted by Mariska Hargitay at 5:00 p.m PT/ 8:00 p.m. ET on September 14.

title: Betty Gilpin Recites “Manic Poem” To Accept First Emmy For ‘Widow’s Bay’: “Let’s All Lean Towards Sam Shepard & Less Toward Sam Altman”
summary: Betty Gilpin capped a stellar night for breakout Apple TV series Widow’s Bay on Sunday by winning the Emmy in the Guest Actress In a Comedy Series category for playing one of the most dramatic — and tragic — characters in the horror comedy: the 18th century Sarah Westcott Warren. Taking the stage on Night […]
content:
Betty Gilpin capped a stellar night for breakout Apple TV series Widow’s Bay on Sunday by winning the Emmy in the Guest Actress In a Comedy Series category for playing one of the most dramatic — and tragic — characters in the horror comedy: the 18th century Sarah Westcott Warren.

Taking the stage on Night 2 of the 2026 Emmys, Gilpin delivered one of the more unusual acceptance speeches, reading a long poem she had written on her phone. It reflected on her journey in acting.

“I want to thank all of the actors I’ve met, old ladies in dressing rooms, hot guys on sets./What a privilege to spend this life laughing at crafty, watching Shakespeare in theaters, half-full and drafty./Our business is stupid, but actors are the bomb. From [Margo] Martindale to [Cristin] Milioti,” Gilpin said, referencing two other Emmy winners, her Mrs. Davis co-star Martindale and longtime best friend Milioti with whom she starred in an off-Broadway play 15 years ago.

Watch on Deadline

Gilpin culminated her speech by urging her fellow artists, “Let’s all lean towards Sam Shepard, and less toward Sam Altman,” to cheers from the audience at the Peacock Theater.

Backstage, Gilpin shared the inspiration for her speech, and it involved fellow Widow’s Bay guest acting Emmy nominee Hamish Linklater, who plays Gilpin’s husband on the show.

“I was on the same flight as my co-nominee Hamish Linklater. He came over to my row and asked if I had written my speech,” Gilpin said. “I was like, ‘No, I’m not going to win.’ He’s like, ‘Well, you need to do that because it’s a scientific possibility, and don’t be stupid just prepare something.’ He scared the sh*t out of me, so I wrote a quick manic poem, which, as you know, women have done for centuries.”

The Guest Actress In a Comedy Series category staged the first major face-off between the two comedy series frontrunners this year, newbie Widow’s Bay and HBO Max’s departing juggernaut Hacks, with the latter’s Kaitlin Olson leading most predictions, followed by Gilpin.

It was a big night for Widow’s Bay, which is leading all programs heading into the September 14 main Emmy telecast with eight wins.

Featured in the flashback Widow’s Bay episode “Our History,” Sarah (Gilpin) arrived in 1702 to marry Widow’s Bay founder Richard Warren (Linklater). On the island, she stumbles upon dark secrets, strange illnesses, unexplained disappearances, that she links to her husband and his alleged deal with a demon (and possibly the devil himself).

Horrified, Sarah tried to flee the island with Richard’s children but dies tragically alongside alongside all children, except one.

This was Gilpin’s fourth Emmy nomination; she was nominated three times for Netflix’s GLOW.

title: Linda Cardellini Wins First Emmy For ‘DTF St. Louis’: “A Real Dream Come True”
summary: Linda Cardellini joined her onscreen husband David Harbour from DTF St. Louis in winning her first Emmy Award for her role in the HBO dark comedy series. She rook the trophy Sunday night in the Outstanding Supporting Actress in a Limited or Anthology Series or Movie. “I’m overcome, I’m sorry it’s a little embarrassing, but […]
content:
Linda Cardellini joined her onscreen husband David Harbour from DTF St. Louis in winning her first Emmy Award for her role in the HBO dark comedy series. She rook the trophy Sunday night in the Outstanding Supporting Actress in a Limited or Anthology Series or Movie.

“I’m overcome, I’m sorry it’s a little embarrassing, but this has just been an unbelievable journey,” Cardellini said on stage. “Thank you to everybody along this way, all these years, who helped me get to this moment. A real dream come true, and I appreciate it very much.”

This is Cardellini’s third nomination and first win. She was previously nominated for the Outstanding Lead Actress in a Comedy Series category for Netflix’s Dead to Me and Outstanding Guest Actress in a Drama Series for AMC’s Mad Men.

Watch on Deadline

“One of my friends once told me it’s a long life in this business if they’re lucky, and I feel very lucky to be here right now holding this Emmy,” she said backstage.

Cardellini also described how she felt walking onstage when her name was called as the winner.

“My heart was beating so fast and I just wanted to be able to feel it and look out and see people and to be able to look out and see so many of my castmates nominated,” she said.

Harbour was one of three DTF St. Louis nominees for Supporting Actor In a Limited or Anthology Series of Movie along with Jason Bateman and Richard Jenkins; Cardellini was nominated on the distaff side alongside Joy Sunday.

RELATED: David Harbour Wins First Emmy For ‘DTF St. Louis’, Thanks HBO For “All Your Tons Of Notes”

In a departure from past years, the supporting acting awards in the limited series category were handed out during Emmys Night 2 (which was formerly referred to as the Creative Arts Emmys), ahead of the primetime ceremony and telecast September 14. Cardellini’s speech was not televised.

DTF St. Louis follows a love triangle between three adults (Harbour, Cardellini, Bateman) experiencing middle-age malaise that leads to one of them ending up dead.

The dark comedy has 13 nominations at the 78th Primetime Emmy Awards; it was a big winner Sunday with six Emmys, including writing and directing.

Come next Monday, DTF St. Louis is also up for Outstanding Limited or Anthology Series during the primetime ceremony and telecast.

title: Rob Reiner Wins Posthumous Emmy Award For ‘The Bear’
summary: In his last major TV role before his death, Rob Reiner did a three-episode arc on Season 4 of FX’s The Bear. On Sunday, the late filmmaker won an Emmy Award posthumously for his performance in the Guest Actor in a Comedy Series category. No one walked onstage, with presenter Wendi McLendon-Covey accepting the award […]
content:
In his last major TV role before his death, Rob Reiner did a three-episode arc on Season 4 of FX’s The Bear. On Sunday, the late filmmaker won an Emmy Award posthumously for his performance in the Guest Actor in a Comedy Series category.

No one walked onstage, with presenter Wendi McLendon-Covey accepting the award on his behalf by saying to the Peacock Theater audience “We all wish he was here,” as everyone stood up to give Reiner a standing ovation.

The camera cut to Jamie Lee Curtis, who was in the audience. Nominated for her own guest-starring role on The Bear, Curtis was credited by Reiner for encouraging him to accept the offer from the Emmy-winning FX/Hulu comedy-drama.

Watch on Deadline

This is Reiner’s third career Emmy; he also won in 1974 and in 1978 in the Supporting Actor In a Comedy Series field for his signature role on CBS’ All In the Family.

RELATED: Rob Reiner: A Hollywood Legend’s Film & TV Career In Photos

Following his tragic death, Reiner is expected to be featured during the In Memoriam tribute during the main Emmy telecast September 14 on NBC. The Princess Bride and When Harry Met Sally director and his wife Michele were found dead in their home on December 14, 2025, with their son Nick Reiner headed to trial for their murder.

On The Bear, Reiner played Albert Schnur, a restaurant franchiser who mentors Ebraheim (Edwin Lee Gibson), advising him on how to expand The Original Beef sandwich walk-up window.

Following his passing, the Emmy-winning series paid a tribute to Reiner in the series finale which featured line cook Ebra calling Albert with the good news that Carmy (Jeremy Allen White) had agreed to franchise the sandwich shop.

While Albert cannot be heard, Ebra ended their exchange with “As you wish,” a nod to the popular line by Cary Elwes’ Westley character in Reiner’s 1987 classic The Princess Bride.

The Bear, created by Christopher Storer, received eight Emmy nominations for its fourth season; the fifth and final season will be in contention at the 2027 Emmys.

Reiner’s final on-screen performance was a cameo as George Washington in Larry David’s Larry David Life, Larry and the Pursuit of Unhappiness, which ran on HBO this summer.

title: ‘Imperium’ Review: Sergei Loznitsa Brings Together Nearly Three Hours of Italian Footage From the Early 1970s Covering the Vastness of the USSR
summary: In the early 1970s, Italian film crews spread out across the USSR, capturing a vast, multicultural empire few had ever seen in such diversity. From urban commuters to village fêtes, Baku trawlers to Siberian reindeer herders, the cameramen aimed to capture the Soviet polity at a time when Westerners had a gray, monolithic image of […]
content:
In the early 1970s, Italian film crews spread out across the USSR, capturing a vast, multicultural empire few had ever seen in such diversity. From urban commuters to village fêtes, Baku trawlers to Siberian reindeer herders, the cameramen aimed to capture the Soviet polity at a time when Westerners had a gray, monolithic image of what lay behind the Iron Curtain. Granted official permission, they managed to resist any push towards propaganda, even finding ways to slyly critique a system that proclaimed regional autonomy but controlled everything from the Kremlin. While planned as a monumental, multi-chapter TV series, only a few episodes wound up being broadcast on Italian TV, just once, following which the endeavor lay forgotten in the archives. If ever there was a project for Sergei Loznitsa, this was it.

In “Imperium,” working with 60 hours of 16mm, the master documentarian organizes this journey along geographic lines, starting in Moscow and heading east, then doubling back through “the Stans” and the Baltic republics until ending in what was then Leningrad. As with Loznitsa’s past films of this type, some snippets of conversation and music have been added, but otherwise the footage has simply been restored and edited together. What’s revealed is an immense state whose distinct regions still managed to hold onto unique traditions, notwithstanding an incessant centralized proclamation of unity.

Popular on Variety

While “Imperium” can be engrossing, its nearly three-hour running time is felt more than in Loznitsa masterpieces like “Maidan” and “State Funeral.” Perhaps that’s because in those films, one feels the force of history pushing us forward, inexorably heading to a watershed moment whose impact continues to resonate across the decades. With “Imperium,” the motivation is clear yet the concept is more diffuse. It’s also a film which will likely resonate best with those of us old enough to recall how the Soviet Union was discussed in the West at the time, a decade before Ronald Reagan’s “Evil Empire” remark — which simply gave a reductivist Star Wars moniker to the anti-communist propaganda suffusing American-driven global discourse since the end of the Second World War. For Loznitsa, of course, his interest is inside the country rather than how it was perceived from abroad, though it will be impossible for most audiences to separate the two.

The film kicks off with a classic parade in Red Square for the 24th Congress of the Central Committee of the Communist Party, with banners touting the same slogans from the previous forty years about production targets being met ahead of schedule. Next comes the GUM department store and window displays with tuxedos, shiny patent leather shoes and beaded handbags, making us wonder who in early 1970s Moscow was buying such luxury goods. Commercialized religion makes its first appearance with a lively trade in Christmas decorations, one of many reminders that despite an official policy of atheism, certain traditions were allowed to persist. (Vladimir Putin, of course, has done an even better job in harnessing religion to his oligarchic dictatorship.)

From the capital the footage moves east, where consumer goods are far more difficult to obtain. In Suzdal, an old woman washes clothes in an ice hole; shots of Vladimir show a town seemingly unchanged from pre-Revolutionary days; further south, residents come out for a winter carnival whose roots must date long before Leninism arrived. As the cameramen spread east, local customs become stronger: Bactrian camel races near the Mongolian border, reindeer sleds in the Sakha Republic. It’s here in Siberia where the footage most forcefully critiques Soviet policy, as a group of young Caucasian Russians (in classic 1970s fashion) play guitar and sing Russian songs, the local Yakut population looking on from the sidelines, discontented observers of this not-so-subtle form of colonialism.

The greatest takeaway from “Imperium” is just how stubbornly resistant centuries-old traditions were to the Soviet push towards uniformity. People still attended mosques in Bukhara and churches in Etchmiadzin, they held on to ways of life that had not been collectivized by Stalinist dictates. Today, however, rampant capitalism and the internet have changed Russia’s social landscape far more than anything Lenin or Brezhnev could have imagined, turning stubbornly multicultural populations that boldly resisted homogeneity into consumers looking West for their acquisitions.

It’s interesting to imagine what might have happened had Italian TV screened the majority of these films upon release. A sense of what life was really like in the Soviet Union was hard to come by then — in the U.S., a 1977 National Geographic publication “Journey Across Russia: The Soviet Union Today” was the first populist corrective to the sense of a uniform society of collectivized proletariat.

Italy, with its strong communist party, had a different problem, too often refusing to acknowledge Politburo abuses. An interesting companion piece to “Imperium” would be Federico Ferrone and Michele Manzolini’s 2013 documentary “The Train to Moscow: A Journey to Utopia,” also consisting of found footage but earlier, when a party supporter from Emilia Romagna discovered that life in the USSR wasn’t all solidarity and freedom. At the time, his Italian colleagues censored his revelations. All empires peddle utopias, but why do so many people believe them?

title: Festival Leaders Confront Growing Political Pressure at Lumiere Summit: ‘We Don’t Judge Artists by Their Passport’
summary: Political pressure on film and television festivals emerged as a defining theme of a panel discussion Monday at the Lumière Summit in Saint-Paul-de-Vence, France, with Séries Mania general director Laurence Herszberg issuing the session’s most direct call for protection of programming autonomy. “We don’t judge artists by their passport, we judge them by their works,” […]
content:
Political pressure on film and television festivals emerged as a defining theme of a panel discussion Monday at the Lumière Summit in Saint-Paul-de-Vence, France, with Séries Mania general director Laurence Herszberg issuing the session’s most direct call for protection of programming autonomy.

“We don’t judge artists by their passport, we judge them by their works,” Herszberg said.

The panel, titled “Easy to Criticize, Impossible to Replace: Rethinking the Festival” and moderated by Rajendra Roy, chief curator of film at MoMA, brought together festival chiefs from Berlin, Cannes, Toronto, San Sebastián, Annecy, Mumbai, Durban, the Red Sea and South by Southwest. It covered three areas: audiences and community, how festivals relate to the media, and the mounting economic and political strains on festival leadership.

Herszberg was direct on the political pressure facing her and her peers. “We feel more and more under pressure from different groups,” she said. “They might be politicians, they might be just people who disagree with the representation of some countries.” As general director of Séries Mania – a free-access festival with 1,500 seats – she said controlling who walks through the door is not possible. “We have to be protected, and we still have to go on and fight for the artists,” Herszberg said.

Popular on Variety

Cameron Bailey, chief executive of the Toronto Film Festival, which launches its first formal market this year, echoed the sentiment. “Filmmakers are not their nations, and shouldn’t be treated as such by anyone,” Bailey said. He recalled joining TIFF as a programmer in 1990, “at a time when festivals felt like a completely free and open space.” Bailey pointed to TIFF’s Next Wave youth program – now 15 years old – as a long-term investment in building young audiences. “‘Obsession’ became one of the biggest sales at a film festival in a long, long time,” Bailey said, noting that Next Wave participants had championed the title. On the rationale for TIFF’s new market, Bailey said: “The market is also part of that ecosystem – I mean, a terrible way to put it would be that it’s the fertilizer of the ecosystem, but really, it’s what feeds” a constant supply of ambitious films.

Berlinale festival director Tricia Tuttle, whose event drew 450,000 admissions last year, and was at the eye of a political storm, put audience development at the center of her contribution. “The answer for me to all of these challenges is to really think about audiences,” Tuttle said, adding that reaching people who are not yet passionate cinemagoers matters as much as serving those who are.

Cannes president Iris Knobloch pointed to the breadth of her festival’s annual gathering – 40,000 accredited participants from 140 countries, with over 4,000 journalists in attendance. “For me, that is the real shining light on films and the talent all over the world,” Knobloch said.

Faisal Baltyuor, chief executive of the Red Sea Film Foundation, said his organization’s last edition sold out every screening. “We have a lot of creative talents that need that boost to make it to the international stage,” Baltyuor said, noting that 11 films the Foundation supported appeared in Venice and eight were heading to Toronto.

On the festival-press relationship, Peter Debruge – now director of the South by Southwest Film & TV Festival after a 20-year tenure at Variety, the last ten as chief critic – put the case for studio films serving discovery. “The studio-level films are the sizzle that brings the attention, the press, and the audiences to the discoveries,” Debruge said.

Maialen Beloki, deputy director of San Sebastián, pointed to shrinking press resources as a structural problem. “Each year, media send less and less critics to the festival,” Beloki said. She added that the race to break news online carries its own cost. “We are losing our capacity to talk about the films with some time and with some respect,” Beloki said.

Shivendra Singh Dungarpur, founding director of the Film Heritage Foundation and director of the MAMI Festival in Mumbai, said his screenings of restored films regularly attract between 1,000 and 1,400 people and that all MAMI events are free of charge. “I believe that a film festival has to be for everyone,” Dungarpur said. He described the MAMI Independent outreach initiative that partnered with a major cinema chain to bring independent films to cities across India ahead of the festival proper.

Mickaël Marin, from the Annecy Animation Film Festival, said that since his appointment in 2018 he has worked to open Annecy to general audiences beyond its traditional professional base, including through a permanent exhibition space that opened last June. “We have a worldwide community of animation coming here in Annecy, from the school, from the student, up to the platform,” Marin said.

Magdalene Reddy, director of the Durban FilmMart Institute, said the core challenge in Africa is not finding audiences but reaching them in the absence of sufficient cinema infrastructure. “For us, engaging with audiences is really going into the community,” Reddy said.

When moderator Roy closed the session by asking whether festivals could survive without the American industry – demanding a yes or no – Reddy was the only panelist to answer no, while noting that her focus remains squarely on African content.

title: ‘Plaza Catedral’ Director Abner Benaim, Chile’s Daniela Vega and Alfredo Castro Board Fiction Series ‘School of the Americas’ (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Panama’s Abner Benaim has boarded as a co-director of the fiction series “School of the Americas” (“Escuela de las Américas”), which will star two of Chile’s most internationally renowned thespians: Daniela Vega, who headed the Oscar-winning “A Fantastic Woman,) and Alfredo Castro, a Pablo Larrain regular who’s also starred in a slew of Latin American […]
content:
Panama’s Abner Benaim has boarded as a co-director of the fiction series “School of the Americas” (“Escuela de las Américas”), which will star two of Chile’s most internationally renowned thespians: Daniela Vega, who headed the Oscar-winning “A Fantastic Woman,) and Alfredo Castro, a Pablo Larrain regular who’s also starred in a slew of Latin American projects.

The project has been selected for the Co-Production and Financing Forum at Madrid-based confab Iberseries & Platino Industria which takes place Sept. 29-Oct. 2.

Benaim was an obvious addition to the project given its subject matter and setting. “School of the Americas” begins with an exhumation at the site of the 1983 El Jazmín massacre, which yields a graduation photograph of four commandos with their faces scratched out and a pendant stamped Fort Gulick, the U.S. military base in the Panama Canal Zone, site of the infamous U.S. Army School of the Americas.

Popular on Variety

Panamanian-American human rights investigator Inés Vega recognizes the massacre’s signature: counterinsurgency doctrine taught at the School. When someone tries to kill her, the cold case turns personal. Tracking four graduates across three continents, she uncovers what the School really taught – and who is still protecting its legacy.

Benaim joins co-director Oscar Godoy who also has close ties to Larraín, having been first AD on Larraín’s “The Count,” “The Club,” “Neruda,” “No” and “Tony Manero.” Godoy was recently second unit director on Fabula’s “Someone Has to Know,” which ranked among Netflix’s global top ten for non-English-language series.

His feature “Ulysses” screened at a string of festivals, starting with the San Sebastián Film Fest and culminating at Chile’s Santiago Film Fest (Sanfic) where it won Best Chilean Film.

Benaim, Panama’s most internationally renowned filmmaker, has represented his country three times at the Oscars, starting with his documentary “Invasion,” about the U.S. 1989 invasion of Panama, followed by “Yo No Me Llamo Rubén Blades” and “Plaza Catedral,” the latter making the Academy shortlist and earning Benaim a Premios Platino nomination for screenplay. His debut feature “Chance” remains the highest-grossing Panamanian film ever released.

Its producers Seedling Media Productions (Panama) and La Panda Productions (U.S./Spain) are targeting 2028 for principal photography to begin, provided all the financing is in place.

“The School of the Americas was a real school, located in the Panama Canal Zone; for half a century, it taught officers from across Latin America. We are not making a series about monsters — monsters are an alibi. We are making one about a curriculum: the fact that this was written down, graded and taught, and the men who graduated went home and became somebody’s father. Violence isn’t born. It’s taught,” said La Panda’s Guillermo Escalona, co-creator and executive producer alongside Brittany DeVries of Seedling Media.

Escalona, a Spanish-American screenwriter-producer based in Los Angeles, co-founder of La Panda Productions, is the co-creator and co-writer, along with Rhayuela’s Federico Durán, of the late Colombian filmmaker Jaime Osorio Márquez’s posthumous feature “The Awakening.” The supernatural action thriller was completed by Durán and José Luis Rugeles (“Alias Maria” “Rebellion”) after the director’s death following which it world-premiered at the Guadalajara International Film Festival in April, with Latido Films handling sales.

Based in Panama, Seedling Media Productions, founded in 2013 by DeVries, has a varied list of credits that include fiction and documentary features. Among them are crime thriller “Chacalería,” “I Really Love My Husband,” shot in Panama and premiered at SXSW in 2025 and documentaries “Dear Panamá,” “A World Without Orphans” and “Lost Kites,” winner of the Best Documentary Feature at the London Independent Film Awards.

Currently, Seedling is producing “Against No One” (“Denuncia Contra Nadie”), a co-production with Guatemala supported by the Ibermedia Co-Production Fund.

title: Studio TF1 Smashes Doc Records With ‘Leon Marchand: Beyond Gold,’ Rolls Out ‘Surface’
summary: Studio TF1 is celebrating recent successes at home and abroad with Sacha Vucinic and Xavier Marchand’s sports documentary “Leon Marchand: Beyond Gold” and Slimane-Baptiste Berhoun’s mystery drama “Surface.” While the doc series on French Olympic swimming champion Leon Marchand and his life in the wake of four gold-medal wins at the Paris Olympics has scored […]
content:
Studio TF1 is celebrating recent successes at home and abroad with Sacha Vucinic and Xavier Marchand’s sports documentary “Leon Marchand: Beyond Gold” and Slimane-Baptiste Berhoun’s mystery drama “Surface.”

While the doc series on French Olympic swimming champion Leon Marchand and his life in the wake of four gold-medal wins at the Paris Olympics has scored record viewing results for France TV, “Surface” has proved a hot seller across Europe and in the U.S.

Offering an intimate look at the young Marchand over the year following his Olympic victories, “Leon Marchand: Beyond Gold” goes beyond the medals to explore his identity, ambition and life as he copes with sudden fame, pursues engineering studies and navigates personal growth at age 22.

Popular on Variety

Setting an all-time documentary record for France TV, the three-part series drew 2.3 million average views per episode when it premiered on the france.tv platform in July followed by 1.6 million viewers on France 2 during its Sept. 1 TV premiere and a total of more than 13 million views across social media, including more than 1 million views on YouTube.

‘Surface’ Baptiste Langinier/France Télévisions/Quad Drama

On the scripted front, Studio TF1’s hit mystery drama “Surface,” which premiered last year at Canneseries and went on to become a major hit on France TV’s streaming platform, has found enthusiastic buyers abroad.

Based on the bestselling novel by Olivier Norek and produced by Quad Drama for France TV, the show has sold to MHz Choice in the U.S., the BBC in the U.K., AMC Global Media in Spain, Vodafone for Greece, Blue Play for French-speaking Switzerland and to Moment in a deal covering airlines and cruise ships.

Also presented last year at the Unifrance Rendez-Vous in Le Havre, the six-part series follows Parisian police captain Noémie Chastain, who is visiting a remote town to assess a police station’s possible closure while recovering from a traumatic facial injury.

When the discovery of a child’s remains leads to the reopening a 20-year-old missing person’s case, Chastain decides to lead the investigation herself, in the process uncovering dark secrets that impact both her and the town.

title: ‘Sumo: Spirit Weighs Nothing’ Review: A Handsome Ode to an Oft-Disrespected Sport
summary: The title of “Sumo: Spirit Weighs Nothing” is the closest that Erik Shirai’s documentary comes to a joke at the expense of its subject: sumo wrestling, the Japanese sport largely known in the western world for the ample size and minimal clothing of its practitioners, and not an awful lot beyond that. In all other […]
content:
The title of “Sumo: Spirit Weighs Nothing” is the closest that Erik Shirai‘s documentary comes to a joke at the expense of its subject: sumo wrestling, the Japanese sport largely known in the western world for the ample size and minimal clothing of its practitioners, and not an awful lot beyond that. In all other respects, however, this stately, artfully produced film aims to act as a corrective to such cheap, culturally insensitive perceptions. Examining as it does the motivations and ambitions of a number of sumo wrestlers, from grand masters to rising stars, through a solemnly respectful lens, the doc finds humanity and even beauty in what can all too easily be comically framed on screen.

Indeed, the approach of Japanese-American docmaker Shirai (who previously probed a very different Japanese institution in his popular 2015 doc “The Birth of Saké”) is so respectful as to feel a touch sanitized: smoothed-out and simplified for the benefit of Western viewers, to whose perspective the film is mostly tailored. More unsavory aspects of the sport — including controversies over hazing and match-fixing, not to mention its ongoing exclusion of women from competition and ceremonies — are swept aside, while the compelling fact of its declining popularity in Japan is only passingly addressed. Only before the closing credits roll is it revealed how few yokozuna (the name given to men achieving the highest rank in sumo) this century have been homegrown, as Mongolia and the U.S. step into the breach.

Popular on Variety

Shedding more light on such matters would provide a richer context for the film’s reverent celebration of sumo tradition, but many viewers will still find it an illuminating and exquisitely mounted study, ennobling the sport with the sheer, studied splendor of its imagery, captured alternately in atmospherically high-contrast monochrome and tea-stained sepia tones. Produced by ESPN Films, it will doubtless find a dedicated broadcast and streaming viewership following its premiere as the opening film of Venice’s audience-oriented Spotlight competition.

Early on, the camera observes a group of rookie wrestlers, training at the Tokyo stable of 62-year-old Master Sakaigawa, as they collectively recite a pledge to the sport: “We shall uphold our responsibility and duty to to sumo; we shall uphold a strong heart, kindness and courage.” This is followed by a droll shot of trainees all putting their freshly laundered thongs out to dry: For all its earnestness, the film is not without offhand humor. In the house of Sakaigawa, we meet Hiradoumi, a 24-year-old upstart tipped for big things in the ring (or dohyō, to use its proper term), and a great hope for continued Japanese representation in the sport’s top tier. In the same stable, and younger still, is teenager Yonezawaryu, still learning the ropes, and battling doubts over his long-term commitment to sumo after witnessing firsthand the extreme, potentially fatal, physical toll it takes on the body.

At the opposite end of the career scale is Mongolian-born Terunofuji, who at the time of filming was the only practicing yokozuna in sumo, a 10-time title winner considering retirement after 14 years in the sport, five of them at the very top. He is spoken of as a veteran, positively godly in status, though he’s only 33 years old. Age, however, doesn’t mean quite what it does to civilians in a realm where so much transformational strain is placed on the body, and Terunofuji’s is beginning to fail him. “By doing sumo, I’m cutting my lifespan by 10 to 20 years,” he frankly admits, before likening the travails of the professional wrestler to those of a soldier going to war. He’s now married with a son — it’s hard not to wonder if, at the end of his reign, he thinks it was all worth it.

It’s one of a few questions that this handsome, sober documentary is too polite to ask. But it does convey the grand, challenging physicality of sumo, which to many of its students qualifies as an answer in itself. There’s also a thoughtful focus here on the pain and labor that goes into building and maintaining these extraordinary bodies — shot, by Shirai and fellow DP Hiroshi Hara, in awed chiaroscuro portraits that line up with the men’s view of themselves as warriors of a kind, leaving far behind many racist, cartoonish depictions of yore.

title: ‘SNL UK’ Adds Comedian & ‘Big Boys’ Actor Freddie Meredith To Season 2 Cast
summary: Saturday Night Live UK has added Such Brave Girls and Big Boys actor Freddie Meredith to the cast of the upcoming second season. Meredith, who is also a comedian, is coming off his Edinburgh Fringe debut show Need a Light?, which was nominated for a Best Newcomer Award. He will now join an ensemble also […]
content:
Saturday Night Live UK has added Such Brave Girls and Big Boys actor Freddie Meredith to the cast of the upcoming second season.

Meredith, who is also a comedian, is coming off his Edinburgh Fringe debut show Need a Light?, which was nominated for a Best Newcomer Award.

He will now join an ensemble also including Hammed Animashaun, Ayoade Bamgboye, Larry Dean, Celeste Dring, George Fouracres, Ania Magliano, Annabel Marlow, Al Nash, Jack Shep, Emma Sidi and Paddy Young.

Meredith said it was a “no brainer” to join SNL UK, calling it, “The most iconic comedy show,” and adding: “It will undoubtedly inform everything I do for the rest of my career and I can’t wait for the experience.”

As announced last week, Jeff Goldblum will present the first episode of SNL UK Season 2 on Sky this Saturday (September 12), with CMAT the musical guest. Five more episodes will follow weekly until October 24 before a midseason break and a return in “early 2027.”

Watch on Deadline

Season 1 hosts included Tina Fey, Hannah Waddingham, and Nicola Coughlan.

SNL UK is produced by Universal Television Alternative Studio’s UK production team and Broadway Video. Lorne Michaels serves as executive producer. James Longman is lead producer.

Sky unscripted chief Phil Edgar-Jones told delegates at the recent Edinburgh Television Festival that the British remake of the iconic U.S. sketch show could continue beyond the second season.

“We’re in this for the long run, and we’re super proud of it, and super proud of the team,” Edgar-Jones said, adding that he was pleased to have proved the social media “naysayers” wrong – referencing the general feeling from the British public and TV industry prior to the show’s launch that Season 1 would fail.

title: BBC Rejects Complaints It Aired “Too Much” Coverage Of Harry & Meghan’s UK Return
summary: BBC News’ coverage of Prince Harry and Meghan Markle’s decision to move back to the UK prompted viewer complaints. The BBC revealed that audience members contacted the UK broadcaster to raise concerns that it was dedicating “too much” airtime to the Duke and Duchess of Sussex. The BBC did not disclose how many complaints it […]
content:
BBC News’ coverage of Prince Harry and Meghan Markle‘s decision to move back to the UK prompted viewer complaints.

The BBC revealed that audience members contacted the UK broadcaster to raise concerns that it was dedicating “too much” airtime to the Duke and Duchess of Sussex.

The BBC did not disclose how many complaints it received from disgruntled viewers, but rejected the concerns in a notice published on its website.

“We believe our approach to this story was proportionate, offering legitimate analysis of the different implications,” the BBC said.

Watch on Deadline

It continued: “News that the Duke and Duchess of Sussex were moving back to the UK with their children was unexpected, given Prince Harry had stated in a BBC interview last year that he didn’t think the family would return due to security concerns.

“This announcement raised several questions, including what prompted this decision, what roles they would fulfil once back in the country, how their security would be funded, how they would navigate dealing with the British media, and what affect this move would have on family relations between the Sussexes and the wider royal family. We gave appropriate scrutiny to these issues, reflecting the context in which they occur.”

Coverage was fueled by speculation that Markle was returning to the UK to pursue an acting opportunity. Deadline reported that the Duchess was in talks to star in Season 3 of The Gentlemen, but this is yet to be confirmed. Commenting on the speculation last month, Manda Levin, Netflix’s scripted chief in the UK, said: “All bets are off.”

The BBC added: “While there was audience interest in this story, with articles about the couple’s return being amongst the most read on our website over the last two weeks, we appreciate not everyone would share this view. We continued to report on many other stories of national and international significance.”

title: BBC News Presenter Maryam Moshiri Reveals She Has Incurable Blood Cancer
summary: Maryam Moshiri, one of the BBC’s most seasoned news presenters, has revealed that she has been diagnosed with blood cancer. In interviews with BBC News and The Times of London, Moshiri said that she is living with polycythaemia vera, a rare but treatable blood cancer. Moshiri, 49, was diagnosed in November 2024 after her doctor […]
content:
Maryam Moshiri, one of the BBC’s most seasoned news presenters, has revealed that she has been diagnosed with blood cancer.

In interviews with BBC News and The Times of London, Moshiri said that she is living with polycythaemia vera, a rare but treatable blood cancer.

Moshiri, 49, was diagnosed in November 2024 after her doctor was “fastidious” about blood tests. Moshiri said she “mostly” had no symptoms, though the condition can cause headaches, confusion, dizziness, and blurred vision.

Polycythaemia vera is manageable with treatment. Moshiri has received “debilitating” rounds of venesection, which involves bloodletting. She has also received immunotherapy.

The cancer can thicken the blood, increasing the risk of developing blood clots that can lead to strokes, heart attacks, or deep vein thrombosis.

Watch on Deadline

“It’s been two years since my diagnosis and I’ve felt that I’ve started to understand the disease a lot better and the way it affects my life. I’ve got a handle on it to a degree now, so I felt it was really important to raise awareness,” Moshiri told BBC News.

On the venesection treatment, she said: “In about a space of five months, I had venesection seven or eight times. So you can imagine my iron levels hit the floor and I felt even more exhausted.

“After a while, I started feeling extremely unwell and tired. I started losing my hair, I got itchy all over my body, but the main symptom was fatigue.”

She continued: “It’s the kind of fatigue that is not like I’m just tired and I didn’t get a good night’s sleep, you feel like someone has removed your battery completely, and however much sleep you get makes no difference.”

Moshiri has continued to work over the past two years, traveling overseas to anchor BBC News, including spending time in Qatar at the start of the U.S.-Israel war with Iran.

“Even though I feel the best I have in two years, I don’t know how I’m going to be in six months, one year, two years,” she said. “People with PV have a higher chance of stroke, heart attack or DVT, so it’s something I always have to be aware of and make sure I mitigate.”

title: Dori Media Wants Buyers To Hunt ‘New Love’ At MIPCOM

content:
EXCLUSIVE: Buyers seeking romance will have a chance for New Love at MIPCOM.

Dori Media Group is launching Fremantle-owned Abot Hameiri‘s new dating format to the international TV marketplace ahead of MIPCOM.

The show puts four single women into accelerated 72-hour live-in situations with carefully selected strangers – moving past dating apps and manufactured first dates directly into daily life: waking up together, meeting friends and family and dealing with everyday moments. After 72 hours, each woman decides to continue for another round, or start again with someone new.

While the show is just hitting the market now, it has been on Reshet 13 in Israel for five seasons already as Ahava Hadasha, with each growing ratings. The fifth season saw the overall audience up by 40% and the 25-34 demographic jumped 250% compared to season three. A sixth season is currently in pre-production.

Watch on Deadline

“We are thrilled to bring Abot Hameiri’s ‘New Love’ to the global TV marketplace,” said Dori Media Group CEO Nadav Palti. “The numbers speak for themselves – five consecutive seasons of growth, and a format that has proven it can hook the younger demographic that every broadcaster is chasing.”

“Dating shows have been selling foreplay for 25 years, New Love sells the relationship,” added Roee Strikovski, CEO of Abot Hameiri. “That’s the whole idea. We put four women straight into real life — 72 hours of actual daily life together, no filters, no isolation. Turns out, that’s where you actually find out if it works. Five seasons of Israeli audiences agree.”

Abot Hamieri is the production company behind Power Couple, the dating format that has launched in more than 25 territories, including a first-ever 24/7 version that debuted this spring across Televisa/Univision’s platforms in the U.S. Hispanic market and Mexico.

Abot Hameiri and Dori Media’s game show The Auction recently launched on América Televisión in Peru.

The news comes as sales houses begin to gear up for MIPCOM, which will be held in just over a month in Cannes, France.

title: Gaza Cinema Academy Launches At Venice Film Festival To Help Gazans Tell Their Own Stories
summary: The official launch of the Gaza Cinema Academy was announced at the Venice Film Festival on Monday, as the humanitarian crisis in the Palestinian territory continues to dominate global news. The initiative – co-founded by Palestinian filmmakers Ezzaldeen Shalh and Mai Masri – aims to establish a sustainable space for film education, training and production […]
content:
The official launch of the Gaza Cinema Academy was announced at the Venice Film Festival on Monday, as the humanitarian crisis in the Palestinian territory continues to dominate global news.

The initiative – co-founded by Palestinian filmmakers Ezzaldeen Shalh and Mai Masri – aims to establish a sustainable space for film education, training and production in the Gaza Strip.

Gaza-based director and film academic Shalh is known for works such as The Dry Spring, The Other World and Love and Bread as well as for spearheading the Gaza International Women’s Film Festival.

“In Gaza, cinema is not merely an art form; it is a means of preserving memory, reclaiming our right to shape our own image, and giving a new generation the tools to tell its own story,” he said.

Watch on Deadline

The launch was accompanied by a short film showing Shalh in the classroom with aspiring female filmmakers talking about their desire to bring their stories to the big screen.

Palestinian film and TV heavyweights Annemarie Jacir, Hiam Abbass and Saleh Bakri have gotten behind the initiative, with Egyptian comedian and filmmaker Ramy Youssef, Tunisian The Voice of Hind Rajab director Kaouther Ben Hania, who is in Venice this year as a member of the jury; Italian producer Graziella Bildesheim, and Alaa Karkouti, cofounder of Cairo-based film promotion and talent company Mad Solutions, also lending their support.

The official launch of the academy is the next step in a process that began in 2024 with the development of the Gaza Filmmaking Diploma, a nine-month theoretical and practical filmmaking training which welcomed its first intake of 25 young Palestinian women in March 2026.

The academy is also working to develop a filmmaking degree accredited by Al-Quds Open University, the main higher education institute for Palestinians, with the aim of establishing a sustainable academic pathway for film education in the Gaza Strip.

Palestinian cinema pioneer Masri is best known for her 2015 feature 3000 Nights, which premiered in Toronto and the played numerous festivals worldwide.

“Supporting a new generation of filmmakers in Gaza means giving them a space to express their reality, memory and dreams. We believe that creativity and cinema can empower, preserve human memory, and build bridges that transcend borders,” she said.

Shalh invited film and cultural institutions, festivals, film funds, production companies, filmmakers and related organizations around the world to build partnerships with the Academy, to exchanging expertise, provide resources and professional opportunities.

“We want the Academy to open a window for young people and women in Gaza to learn, create and make their own films, and for their voices and images to reach the world. We invite our partners in institutions, universities and the international film community to be part of building this space,” he said.
